title: 191. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Solving Three-by-Three Linear Systems by Elimination
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three linear system by eliminating one variable.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=6\\
x-y+z=2\\
x+y-z=0
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Subtract the second equation from the first: \((x+y+z)-(x-y+z)=6-2\), so \(2y=4\) and \(y=2\). Add the first and third equations: \((x+y+z)+(x+y-z)=6+0\), so \(2x+2y=6\). With \(y=2\), this gives \(2x+4=6\), so \(x=1\). Substitute into the first equation: \(1+2+z=6\), so \(z=3\). The solution is \((1,2,3)\).
questions.hint: Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate \(x\) and \(z\) and find \(y\), then add the first and third equations to eliminate \(z\).

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three linear system by eliminating one variable and then a second variable.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=9\\
x-y+z=5\\
x+y-z=3
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Subtract the second equation from the first: \(2y=4\), so \(y=2\). Add the first and third equations: \(2x+2y=12\), so with \(y=2\), \(2x+4=12\), giving \(x=4\). Substitute into the first equation: \(4+2+z=9\), so \(z=3\). The solution is \((4,2,3)\).
questions.hint: Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate \(x\) and \(z\) and find \(y\), then add the first and third equations to eliminate \(z\).

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three linear system by first eliminating two variables at once.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
2x+y+z=8\\
x-y+z=0\\
x+y-z=4
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Add the second and third equations: \((x-y+z)+(x+y-z)=0+4\), so \(2x=4\) and \(x=2\). Substitute \(x=2\) into the first equation: \(4+y+z=8\), so \(y+z=4\). Substitute \(x=2\) into the second equation: \(2-y+z=0\), so \(z=y-2\). Then \(y+(y-2)=4\), giving \(2y=6\), so \(y=3\) and \(z=1\). The solution is \((2,3,1)\).
questions.hint: Add the second and third equations to eliminate both \(y\) and \(z\) and find \(x\) first.

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Reduce a three-by-three system to a two-by-two system by elimination.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=7\\
2x-y+z=7\\
x+2y-z=0
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Add the first and third equations: \(2x+3y=7\). Add the second and third equations: \(3x+y=7\). From \(3x+y=7\), \(y=7-3x\). Substitute into \(2x+3y=7\): \(2x+3(7-3x)=7\), so \(2x+21-9x=7\), giving \(-7x=-14\) and \(x=2\). Then \(y=7-3(2)=1\). Substitute into the first equation: \(2+1+z=7\), so \(z=4\). The solution is \((2,1,4)\).
questions.hint: Add the first and third equations, then add the second and third equations, to reduce the system to two equations in \(x\) and \(y\).

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three linear system by forming two new equations that eliminate the same variable.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=6\\
2x-y+z=7\\
x+2y-z=3
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Add the first and third equations: \(2x+3y=9\). Add the second and third equations: \(3x+y=10\). From \(3x+y=10\), \(y=10-3x\). Substitute into \(2x+3y=9\): \(2x+3(10-3x)=9\), so \(2x+30-9x=9\), giving \(-7x=-21\) and \(x=3\). Then \(y=10-3(3)=1\). Substitute into the first equation: \(3+1+z=6\), so \(z=2\). The solution is \((3,1,2)\).
questions.hint: Form two new equations by adding the first with the third, and the second with the third, so that \(z\) is eliminated.

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Apply elimination to solve a three-by-three system after eliminating one variable.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=9\\
x-y+z=3\\
2x+y-z=3
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Subtract the second equation from the first: \((x+y+z)-(x-y+z)=9-3\), so \(2y=6\) and \(y=3\). Add the first and third equations: \((x+y+z)+(2x+y-z)=9+3\), so \(3x+2y=12\). With \(y=3\), \(3x+6=12\), giving \(x=2\). Substitute into the first equation: \(2+3+z=9\), so \(z=4\). The solution is \((2,3,4)\).
questions.hint: Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate \(x\) and \(z\) and find \(y\), then add the first and third equations to eliminate \(z\).

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three linear system by comparing two expressions for the same variable.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=6\\
2x+y-z=3\\
x-y+2z=2
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Add the first and second equations: \(3x+2y=9\). Add the second and third equations: \(3x+z=5\), so \(z=5-3x\). From the first equation, \(z=6-x-y\). Equate the two expressions for \(z\): \(6-x-y=5-3x\), so \(2x-y=-1\), or \(y=2x+1\). Substitute into \(3x+2y=9\): \(3x+2(2x+1)=9\), so \(3x+4x+2=9\), giving \(7x=7\) and \(x=1\). Then \(y=2(1)+1=3\) and \(z=6-1-3=2\). The solution is \((1,3,2)\).
questions.hint: Combine equations to eliminate \(z\), then express one variable in terms of another.

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a symmetric three-by-three system by first adding all equations.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
2x+y+z=8\\
x+2y+z=7\\
x+y+2z=9
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Add all three equations: \(4x+4y+4z=24\), so \(x+y+z=6\). Subtract this sum equation from the first equation: \((2x+y+z)-(x+y+z)=8-6\), so \(x=2\). Subtract the sum equation from the second equation: \((x+2y+z)-(x+y+z)=7-6\), so \(y=1\). Subtract the sum equation from the third equation: \((x+y+2z)-(x+y+z)=9-6\), so \(z=3\). The solution is \((2,1,3)\).
questions.hint: Add the three equations first to obtain a simple equation for \(x+y+z\), then compare it with each original equation.

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three system by subtracting a multiple of one equation from another.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=6\\
2x+3y+2z=14\\
x+2y+3z=16
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Subtract twice the first equation from the second: \((2x+3y+2z)-2(x+y+z)=14-12\), so \(y=2\). Subtract the first equation from the third: \((x+2y+3z)-(x+y+z)=16-6\), so \(y+2z=10\). With \(y=2\), \(2+2z=10\), giving \(z=4\). Substitute into the first equation: \(x+2+4=6\), so \(x=0\). The solution is \((0,2,4)\).
questions.hint: Subtract twice the first equation from the second to eliminate \(x\) and \(z\), then subtract the first equation from the third to eliminate \(x\).

questions.concept: Solving a three-by-three linear system by elimination
questions.learningObjective: Solve a three-by-three system by eliminating a variable through strategic equation addition.
questions.question:
Solve the system
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=4\\
2x-y+z=1\\
3x+y-z=4
\end{cases}
\]
by elimination.
questions.explanation: Add the first and third equations: \((x+y+z)+(3x+y-z)=4+4\), so \(4x+2y=8\), or \(2x+y=4\). Add the second and third equations: \((2x-y+z)+(3x+y-z)=1+4\), so \(5x=5\) and \(x=1\). Then \(2(1)+y=4\), so \(y=2\). Substitute into the first equation: \(1+2+z=4\), so \(z=1\). The solution is \((1,2,1)\).
questions.hint: Add the first and third equations to eliminate \(z\), and add the second and third equations to eliminate both \(y\) and \(z\).
